summary: Horizon Mask is a web app that compares lunar landing sites and dates on one screen. For each site it shows when the Sun is above the terrain (power) and when Earth is above the terrain (direct-to-Earth communication), using NASA LOLA elevation data and checked against JPL Horizons. At the south pole a small hill or a one-week delay can end a mission; Horizon Mask lets planners see that in seconds.
details:
What it does. Choose from 15 notable sites (Apollo, CLPS, Chandrayaan-3, Chang'e, SLIM and south-pole candidates) or enter coordinates. Pick a start date and a span of 30 days, 3 months or a year. The app computes hourly Sun and Earth azimuth and elevation at every site and reports:

  • share of time with power, with comms, and with both
  • longest continuous operations window and longest stretch without power
  • at the time cursor: Sun and Earth height above terrain, and time to the next sunset or Earthset
  • a timeline of Power, Comms and Ops bars per site, which can be scrubbed or animated
  • a horizon panorama and compass showing the Sun and Earth against the terrain outline

How it works. The work is split in two so the interface stays instant.

  1. Horizon mask (offline, Python). For a site, every pixel of a LOLA elevation model within range is converted to an azimuth and an elevation angle as seen from the site, and the highest value per degree of azimuth is kept. The result is 360 numbers describing the terrain skyline. This vectorised approach replaces 360 separate ray marches.
  2. Ephemeris (in the browser, JavaScript). Sun and Earth positions are computed from analytic lunar theory (truncated ELP-2000/82 and lunar libration formulas from Meeus) in the Mean-Earth / Polar-Axis frame used by LOLA, with a correction for the observer's position on the surface. No server or API call is needed.
  3. Intersection. A body is visible when its elevation exceeds the mask at its azimuth. The Sun is treated as a disk, so power ramps up as the disk clears the terrain rather than switching instantly.
  4. Cross-check. A script pulls the same angles from the JPL Horizons API for flight-grade confirmation.

Validation. The browser engine reproduces a published worked example to 0.01° and agrees with an independent calculation (astropy ephemeris with the IAU 2009 lunar rotation model) to within 0.034° across 3,604 samples from 2026 to 2028. The mask algorithm matches analytic answers on synthetic terrain to 0.01°.

Benefits. When a launch slips, a planner can see in seconds which alternative site or date still has power and comms. Educators can show why polar lighting is so different from the Apollo sites by putting Apollo 11 next to Shackleton.

Limits. Planning-grade accuracy. Without a loaded mask the app assumes a smooth Moon. Comms is geometric line of sight only; diffraction and multipath are not modelled. Polar candidate coordinates are approximate.

Tools and languages. JavaScript, HTML Canvas and CSS for the app, with no framework and no build step. Python with NumPy, rasterio, pyproj and requests for the pipeline; astropy for validation. No hardware.

AI disclosure. Generative AI (Claude, Anthropic) wrote the application code (index.html, engine.js), the Python pipeline scripts, the README, the architecture diagram, the presentation slides and the first draft of this text. The team reviewed and tested the output. Each source file notes this in its header, and each image carries an on-image AI-generated label.
